candidate_relations.reason: CT localizes the abscess to the left lacrimal sac with mainly extraconal postseptal stranding, so an orbital abscess assigns the collection to the wrong compartment and omits the optic-nerve injury.
The acute two-day painful febrile-appearing orbital process with a culture growing Streptococcus pyogenes provides no granulomatous or multisystem evidence for sarcoidosis.
Pan-susceptible S. pyogenes and postseptal fat stranding support streptococcal orbital extension, but this label omits the lacrimal-sac origin and diffusion-proven optic-nerve injury.
Visual loss developed with acute orbital pain and whole-orbital-segment optic-nerve diffusion restriction in a 59-year-old, which is incompatible with amblyopia.
MRI shows acute injury of the entire orbital optic-nerve segment during enlargement of a compressive lacrimal-sac abscess, not a primary demyelinating optic neuritis syndrome.
The CT-demonstrated lacrimal-sac abscess is the suppurative focus of the acute dacryocystitis, but it does not include the secondary optic-nerve injury.
No neuropathy, renal disease, skin findings, or vascular lesions accompany the culture-proven lacrimal infection to suggest polyarteritis nodosa.
Extraconal postseptal stranding and S. pyogenes identify secondary streptococcal orbital cellulitis, whereas the full diagnosis centers on acute dacryocystitis complicated by optic-nerve injury.
Bilateral nasolacrimal-duct opacification and a left lacrimal-sac abscess fit a lacrimal-system disorder, but the label lacks the acute infection and neurologic complication.
A unilateral two-day painful process with a bacterial lacrimal-sac abscess and no thyroid findings is not Graves' orbitopathy.
Isolation of S. pyogenes from an enlarging lacrimal-sac abscess establishes an infectious source rather than idiopathic orbital inflammation.
The patient had no prior dacryocystitis and presented after two days of orbital pain, so chronic dacryocystitis conflicts with the documented acute episode.
Imaging documents an abscess, but the generic term does not specify its lacrimal-sac location, acute dacryocystitis, or associated optic-nerve injury.
Postseptal fat stranding and restricted eye movements show orbital cellulitis as extension from the lacrimal-sac infection, not the complete lacrimal-and-optic-nerve diagnostic object.
MRI/MRA showed a patent ophthalmic artery and the record describes no cavernous-sinus filling defect, cranial-nerve pattern, or intracranial thrombosis.
Marked visual loss and ophthalmoplegia resemble an orbital-apex syndrome, but imaging places the abscess extraconally and shows diffuse orbital optic-nerve injury without an apex lesion.
Hypertension was controlled on lisinopril and does not account for the lacrimal-sac abscess, S. pyogenes culture, or acute optic-nerve injury.
The culture confirms a streptococcal infection, but this label supplies neither the dacryocystitis anatomy nor the secondary optic-nerve complication.
The record contains a localized S. pyogenes lacrimal abscess without sinonasal destruction, pulmonary disease, renal disease, or vasculitic histology expected for granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
Dacryocystitis names the primary process supported by months of epiphora and the lacrimal-sac abscess, but omits its acute state and secondary optic-nerve injury.
